title: Chapter 4: Nothing Gets Stamped Tonight
content: Tuesday the Annex opens at nine and Wren is at the window at eight forty-one, before the lights are on, holding the folder flat against her chest so the corners keep their shape.

By nine there are eleven people behind her. By nine twenty there are twenty-six. The line goes out the door, down the ramp, and stops where the asphalt gives up and the gravel starts, because nobody in this town will stand on the crack.
The ticket machine is bolted to the wall beside the window. It is red and it feeds out a strip of paper that smells like a hardware store. She takes B-014 and sits under the clock.

The Annex was a post office once. There are brass boxes in the wall with numbers on them and no keys in the locks. Above the boxes is a mural of men with shovels on a riverbank, and behind the men is the river with no gate on it, wide and flat and going somewhere.
She has looked at that mural for two days. The men are building something. She cannot tell what.
At nine the bell rings. It rings twice, half a second apart, like it is clearing its throat. The window goes up and Hollis Drane's cardigan appears behind the glass.
He has a mug with a chip in the rim. He has a stamp in his right hand and he does not look up until the board calls a number.
The first one is a man with a fence permit. Hollis reads it, asks one question about the property line, and brings the stamp down. The sound is small and flat. The man takes his paper and goes.
The second is a dog license. The dog is outside on the ramp, tied to the rail, a brown thing with a bad eye. Hollis asks for the rabies certificate. The man has it in a plastic sleeve. Stamp.
Wren counts. She has a pencil and the back of an old receipt and she draws one line for each stamp, and by ten fifteen she has eleven lines and the room smells like wet coats.
A woman comes in with a photograph of a shed.

The shed is twelve by sixteen, unpainted, sitting behind a house on Palmer Road. The woman has a surveyor's sketch, a receipt for lumber, and a letter from a neighbor saying the neighbor does not object. Hollis reads all three. He asks whether the shed has a floor. The woman says it has a floor. He stamps the photograph.
The woman says thank you. She says it twice. She goes out into the rain with the photograph held by one corner like it is still wet.
Wren counts the minutes. Four.

At nine fifty-two her number goes up on the board and she stands too fast and the folder slips and the papers fan out on the floor and she goes down on one knee in front of twenty-six people and picks them up in order.
At the window she says, "Does a Form 9 get a number."
Hollis looks at her over the top of his glasses. "It gets a receipt."
"I want the receipt."

He turns the form over. He writes her name in the box at the top in a hand that leans left, and then he takes the rubber stamp off the pad and brings it down, once on the white copy and once on the yellow.
RECEIVED SEP 15 2026. ANNEX 04. 26-0471.
He tears the yellow along the perforation and pushes it under the glass with two fingers.
It is the first thing in the world with her grandfather's name typed on it. It is yellow and it is thin and it has a number.
"What happens now," she says.
"Intake review."
"How long is intake review."
"That depends." He has already looked past her at the next person. "On the volume."
"Write the date on it."
He looks up.
"On the receipt," she says. "You stamped it. Write the date under the stamp. In pen."

He does it. He does not ask why. She takes the yellow slip and folds it once, along the middle, and puts it in the inside pocket of the jacket, which is her grandfather's jacket, and which still smells like diesel and river.
She sits back down under the clock and counts again.

By noon there are forty lines on the back of the receipt. Forty people in three hours. A fence, a dog, a shed, a septic variance, a driveway culvert, a variance on a setback, a duplicate title, a burn permit for brush, a name change, a birth certificate for a man who is sixty and wants to go to Canada.
Mars texts at noon. Any movement. She writes back, no. Mars writes back, come to the courthouse, I will buy you a sandwich. She writes back, after.
The woman with the tree comes at one.

She is seventy or better, in a raincoat with the hood down, and she has a letter from an arborist and a photograph of a black walnut that is coming apart over her roof. One limb is already down. It is lying across the rhododendrons in the picture, and there is a boy in the picture, holding up two fingers behind the tree.

Hollis reads the letter. He asks how old the tree is. The woman says her father planted it in 1961 and she has the receipt, and she puts the receipt on the counter, and it is a carbon, faded to the color of weak tea.
Hollis reads the receipt. He stamps the letter.
The woman says, "That's it?"
"That's it," Hollis says. "You can take it down Saturday."
She thanks him and goes, and she holds the letter in both hands in front of her like a church program.
Wren is standing at the counter by then, because she has been standing at the counter since one o'clock, and she says, "The tree got a stamp in four minutes."
Hollis does not look up. "The tree had a form."
"So did he."
"The tree had a form with a box on it for the tree."
At one ten Hollis gets up and goes to the second desk, the one behind the half wall where the folders are stacked in leaning towers, and he opens the bottom left drawer.

Wren sees it from where she stands. The drawer is deeper than the desk. There are folders in it standing on their edges, and on each spine is a year, written in marker, 1997, 1998, 1999, and the folders go back further than she can see and forward to a year she cannot read.
He takes out a roll of tape. He puts nothing in. He closes the drawer with his knee.
At three ten a girl of nineteen or twenty comes in with a form already filled out and gets sent back to the rack by the window, and comes back with the same form, and is sent back again.

Wren is standing by the rack. She has read every tab on it in two days, first out of boredom and then out of habit. The girl has 8B, Application for Correction of Name, and she has ticked 8B-3, which is for a clerical error made by the county.
"Not that one," Wren says. "You want 8C. The green one. If the mistake was yours, it's 8C, and you have to say it was yours, in the box at the bottom, in your own words."
The girl looks at her. "They didn't say that."
"They won't," Wren says. "They'll just hand it back."
The girl takes 8C off the rack and fills it in standing up against the window ledge, and Hollis stamps it at three forty, and on her way out she stops and says, "How did you know that."
"I read the rack," Wren says.
The girl nods slowly, like she is memorizing it, and goes out into the rain with the paper inside her coat.

She does not go. She stays until the window closes at four thirty and the lights in the back go off one bank at a time, and then she walks home along the river road with the receipt in her pocket and her hand flat over it.
Wednesday she is back at eight fifty and takes B-009 and sits in the same chair.
Five hours this time. She has brought a sandwich and a bottle of water and she does not eat the sandwich.

She learns the order of things. Hollis stamps, then writes. Never writes, then stamps. When he is unsure he takes the paper into the back room and comes out without it. When he is sure he stamps it and the person leaves happy and the next person steps up before the chair is cold.
She learns that the bell rings twice every time the window goes up, and that nobody in the room looks at it except her.

In her notebook, on a clean page, she writes the times in a column. Window up at nine. Window down at twelve. Up at one. Down at four thirty. Six and a half hours of stamping in a day, forty stamps in a morning, and not one of them for a cause.
She writes that down too, in the margin, in smaller letters, because it is the only number in the building that is hers.
She learns that a man can get a stamp for a boat trailer in the time it takes her to write one line on the back of a receipt.

At four fifty the window is down and the chairs are stacked and a woman is running a vacuum over the mat by the door. Hollis comes out from behind the glass with his cardigan buttoned wrong and her folder in his hand.
He stops in front of her. He does not sit.
"Mrs. Aubrey," he says.
She lets it stand. Nobody has called her that before. Her mother was Mrs. Aubrey. She is not sure it is hers.
"Your file," he says. "It has been routed."
She waits.
"It went out Monday night. It has been routed upstairs."
She looks at the folder in his hand, which is the folder he took from her, which has her name on the tab in his leaning hand.
"Upstairs is the mezzanine," she says. "I have been on the mezzanine. It's a copier and a lunchroom."
Hollis looks at the mat. The vacuum goes over the same square of carpet twice.
"Upstairs is Columbus," he says.
She stands there with the vacuum noise in her ears.

"Everything with a cause in it goes to Columbus," he says. "Fence posts stay here. Trees stay here. A cause goes to Columbus, and Columbus has thirty days, and after thirty days Columbus has thirty more, and I do not have a number for Columbus. I have a mailbox."

He hands her nothing. He puts the folder under his arm and buttons the top button of his cardigan and starts to say the sentence, the one she has already heard once, and she watches him decide not to.
"I'll come Friday," she says.
"Friday's fine," Hollis says, and goes out the side door into the rain, and the door closes slowly on its spring, and the vacuum goes over the same square of carpet a third time.
highlight: Waiting at the window, Wren watches forty small permits get stamped while her grandfather's death does not.
